lead: Both readings are about the single aim that gives order to the whole of life. Paul says that whatever we do, we should do it for the glory of God, and that he himself imitates Christ. In Luke, Jesus speaks to large crowds and says that to follow him costs everything, as a builder or a king must count the cost before beginning. The day also names St Ignatius of Loyola, whose motto was the greater glory of God. The key words are for the glory of God and count the cost.

r.h: Do everything for the glory of God
set: Paul closes a long answer (8:1–11:1) to the Corinthians’ question about eating meat that has been offered to idols. His answer is balanced: idols are nothing, but the weak may be hurt if the strong use their freedom without love. Many in the city bought meat from temple markets, and a meal in a friend’s house could easily raise the question.

Our verses give the summary. All of life, the plainest acts such as eating and drinking, is to be offered to God, and in whatever he does Paul seeks the good of others so that they may be saved. The chapter division is unfortunate: the first verse of chapter 11 belongs to the argument of chapter 10.
str: v. 31: whether you eat or drink, do everything for the glory of God.
v. 32: give no offense to Jews, to Greeks or to the church of God.
v. 33: Paul’s own practice: not seeking his own advantage but that of many.
11:1: be imitators of me, as I am of Christ.
kw: The weight and radiance of God. To do something “for the glory of God” is to let his goodness show in it.
Literally “not causing to stumble”. The word recalls the stumbling block that Paul fears to put before a weaker believer (8:9).
Paul asks to be imitated only as he imitates Christ. The standard is Christ, and the apostle is a pointer.
vv: do everything for the glory of God.
Nothing is too small. Eating, drinking and the ordinary acts of the day can be given to God.
Give no offense to Jews or to Greeks or to the church of God
Paul names the three groups of his world: Jews, Gentiles and the Church. He wants to cause no needless stumbling to any.
Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ.
Christianity is learned by following people who follow Christ. Parents, catechists and pastors are all asked to be this kind of example.
ch: The Church takes up Paul’s verse as the principle of the whole Christian life: every act, offered to God, becomes prayer. The Catechism teaches that the glory of God consists in the manifestation and communication of his goodness, for which the world was created (CCC 294). It also puts before us the saints as models and intercessors (CCC 828). In the Eastern tradition, the whole day, with its meals and its work, is surrounded with the prayers of the hours.

set: Jesus is on the road to Jerusalem, and large crowds travel with him (14:25). He turns and tells them what following him means. The language is deliberately sharp. Just before this he has told of the great banquet to which many make excuses (14:15–24), and now he warns those who join the journey that it is not a casual walk.

“Hate” in verse 26 is Semitic speech: to love less by comparison. Matthew gives the sense: “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (10:37). Jesus does not teach contempt for family, which the fourth commandment honours. He asks that no bond come before him. Then come two small parables, the builder and the king, both about thinking ahead before starting.
str: v. 25: large crowds with him on the road.
vv. 26–27: no one can be a disciple who puts even family or life before him, or who will not carry the cross.
vv. 28–30: the tower builder: count the cost first.
vv. 31–32: the king: weigh your strength before going to war.
v. 33: so none can be a disciple who does not give up all possessions.
kw: In biblical Hebrew and Aramaic “hate” can mean “love less” or “prefer something else”, as in Genesis 29:30–31 where Leah is “hated” in comparison with Rachel.
Literally to count with pebbles. The builder sits down and reckons honestly. Discipleship is not an impulse; it is a considered, lasting decision.
to say farewell, to give up
A word used for taking leave of someone. Disciples take leave of everything that would rule them.
vv: Whoever comes to me and does not hate father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, yes, and even life itself, cannot be my disciple.
The sentence is shocking on purpose, to show the place of Christ. Those who love him most also love their families best, because they love them in him.
Whoever does not carry the cross and follow me cannot be my disciple.
Every disciple has a cross. Jesus does not hide it. It is carried behind him, never alone.
which of you, intending to build a tower, does not first sit down and estimate the cost
Jesus encourages planning. A well-built life asks for clear thought and honest prayer.
none of you can become my disciple if you do not give up all your possessions.
To give up is to hold nothing as one’s own security. Some are called to leave everything; all are called to hold everything lightly.
ch: The Catechism teaches that detachment from riches is necessary for entering the kingdom of heaven (CCC 2544), and that the bonds of the family are not absolute, for the child’s first loyalty is to God (CCC 2232). The tradition has understood the words as the call of every Christian, and as the source of the counsels of poverty, chastity and obedience in the religious life. The two parables remind us that the response to Christ is made with open eyes. The cross that Jesus asks us to carry is in the end the road to joy.

qa: Does Jesus really ask us to hate our families?

No. The word is a Semitic way of saying “love less than”, as Matthew’s parallel shows (10:37). Jesus himself honoured his mother and gave her to the beloved disciple from the cross (John 19:26–27). What he asks is that no loyalty, even the dearest, stand in the way of following him. In practice, those who put Christ first become better sons, daughters, spouses and parents.
rite: The day also names St Ignatius of Loyola (1491–1556), a Basque soldier who was wounded in battle, read the lives of Christ and the saints during his recovery, and gave his life to God. He founded the Society of Jesus, whose motto is “for the greater glory of God”. His own life shows both of today’s readings: the call to do everything for God’s glory and the cost of leaving the old way of living for Christ. Many Jesuit missionaries, among them St Francis Xavier, a companion of Ignatius, came to India.
study: Paul asks us to do everything for the glory of God, even eating and drinking. What ordinary part of my day could I deliberately offer to God this week?
Jesus asks the builder to count the cost. What might I need to give up or hold more lightly so that I can follow him more fully and with an undivided heart?
